# AI Product Engineering Owner — 10-day learning path (summary)

> Source: `ai-product-engineering-owner-10-day-learning-path.pdf` (Nebinfra Technologies, APSO-10D-2026-001, 2026-09-20, private and confidential).
> Prose is condensed; tables, day tests, AI prompts, and scoring rules are reproduced verbatim.

## Mission

In ten business days, build the evidence needed to qualify for an AI-native product engineering role (the next generation of the AI Forward Engineer) and prepare for formal onboarding. AI agents do a growing share of research, coding, testing, and analysis; you remain accountable for every decision and result.

- **10** business days · **1** synthetic capstone · **100** readiness points · **80** minimum passing score
- Operating principle: *AI can multiply execution. It does not transfer accountability.*
- A Day 10 pass qualifies you for the role; it does not certify independent product ownership. Detailed NebCore training belongs to formal onboarding.

## The role you are preparing for

| Responsibility | The question you must answer |
|---|---|
| Product outcome | What problem are we solving, for whom, and how will success be measured? |
| Product contract | What must the user experience, including loading, empty, failure, and recovery states? |
| Architecture | Where does authority live, how does data move, and how does the system fail? |
| AI engineering | What may agents do, what evidence must they return, and where must a human decide? |
| Delivery | How does an accepted decision become a reviewed, deployed, verified change? |
| Operations | Is the product healthy, secure, affordable, supportable, and improving? |

**Ownership loop:** 01 Discover (user, work, constraint, business result) → 02 Decide (freeze experience, contract, architecture, risks) → 03 Direct (AI agents get bounded objectives and evidence requirements) → 04 Prove (review, test, deploy, trace real behavior) → 05 Improve (measure outcomes, reliability, cost, learning).

## Daily operating rhythm

Full-time intensive, eight focused hours per day.

| Time | Activity | Daily evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 90 minutes | Learn the day's concepts from primary sources | Notes and concept check |
| 3 hours | Build the required capstone slice | Working implementation |
| 90 minutes | Direct an AI agent on bounded work | Task contract and transcript summary |
| 60 minutes | Review AI output adversarially | Findings and corrections |
| 60 minutes | Test and trace the real path | Test result and runtime evidence |
| 30 minutes | Explain the learning back | Short written or recorded teach-back |

Every day ends with a usable artifact. Reading without building does not count as completion.

## Local workstation requirement

All hosting, test traffic, storage, identity simulation, deployment, and operational evidence run on the laptop. No public cloud, hosted DB/object store/identity, remote runtime, public webhook relay, or deployment platform. Internet only for docs, package downloads, the personal GitHub repo + GitHub Actions CI, and an authorized Claude Code or Codex CLI subscription. GitHub stores source, docs, reviews, CI — never the app, its data, model, or runtime dependencies. macOS and Linux only (no Windows, no WSL).

### Laptop capacity

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | 8 logical cores | 12 or more logical cores |
| Memory | 16 GB | 32 GB or more |
| Free SSD space | 60 GB | 100 GB or more |
| Architecture | Apple silicon, x86_64, or Linux arm64 | Apple silicon or Linux x86_64 with supported GPU |
| Network | Internet during setup | Internet during setup; offline-capable during daily tests |

At 16 GB run only the day's services; at 32 GB+ the full stack. Record actual peak memory, disk use, and service startup time during preflight.

### Required local tools

| Area | Required tools | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Shell and source | Bash or Zsh, Git, GitHub CLI, Make, curl, jq, OpenSSL | Automation, version control, pull requests, API probes, JSON processing, signatures |
| Frontend | Current Node.js LTS, Corepack, pnpm, browser developer tools | React build and simple browser checks |
| Backend | Current stable Go toolchain | API, worker, tests, profiling |
| Utility scripting | Python 3.12 or newer and uv | Local scripts, fixtures, JSONL validation |
| Containers | Docker Engine with Compose v2 | All stateful and supporting services |
| AI engineering CLI | Claude Code or Codex CLI with an active authorized subscription | Daily AI engineering sessions and native transcript capture |
| Local checks | Browser, curl, jq, shell scripts, standard project test commands | Simple repeatable behavior and failure checks |

Pin versions (project files or version manager); record every installed version in `workstation-versions.txt`. No unpinned `latest` container tags in submitted work.

### Required personal GitHub repository

Create before Day 1 (private preferred); grant the assessor read access before first submission.

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | Local setup, start, stop, test, reset, and assessment instructions |
| `apps/` | Frontend and Go API source |
| `services/` | Worker and local provider stub |
| `deploy/compose.yaml` | Complete laptop-hosted runtime |
| `docs/day-01/` through `docs/day-10/` | Daily inputs, JSONL, artifacts, review, score, and teach-back |
| `tests/` | Simple local end-to-end and failure simulations |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Required CI workflow |

CI must run formatting or lint checks, frontend tests, Go tests, OpenAPI validation, a production build, and JSONL submission validation. CI must not deploy anything, call a hosted model, or require production credentials; use fixtures and deterministic local substitutes.

Daily work: branch `day-N-topic`, one PR into the default branch. The PR links the five daily submission files, reports the measured score, and includes the CI run. Merge only after required checks pass and the daily review is complete.

### Required laptop-hosted services

| Service | Local implementation | Default binding |
|---|---|---|
| Application UI | React development server or local container | 127.0.0.1:3000 |
| Go API | Local process or container | 127.0.0.1:8080 |
| PostgreSQL | Container with host-local volume | 127.0.0.1:5432 |
| Redis | Container with host-local volume | 127.0.0.1:6379 |
| Evidence files | Project-local directory with generated expiring-link simulation | Local filesystem only |
| Identity simulation | Locally signed synthetic tokens issued by a test helper | No separate identity server |
| Capstone AI adapter | Local deterministic stub or recorded fixture | Application tests without a hosted runtime dependency |
| Provider simulation | Candidate-built signed webhook and failure stub | 127.0.0.1:8090 |
| Operational signals | Structured application logs and a local metrics summary file | Local files and terminal output |

Bind ports to `127.0.0.1`, not `0.0.0.0`. Synthetic credentials stored outside source control. Test data and evidence in a deletable project-local directory.

### Local preflight gate

Before Day 1, submit `workstation-preflight.md` with the command and captured result for each check:

1. Confirm the operating system is macOS or Linux and record CPU architecture.
2. Record CPU count, total memory, and free disk space.
3. Record versions of Git, GitHub CLI, Node.js, pnpm, Go, Python, uv, Docker, Compose, the selected AI CLI, curl, and jq.
4. Start a container and prove it is reachable only through loopback.
5. Authenticate Claude Code or Codex CLI with the candidate's subscription, complete one test session, and locate its native transcript or JSONL export.
6. Build the application images locally and start them with Docker Compose without pulling application images from a remote registry.
7. Start PostgreSQL and Redis; verify health and local persistence. Create the evidence directory and a synthetic signed-token fixture.
8. Prove that all application endpoints resolve to loopback or the private Compose network and that no runtime configuration names an external service.
9. Create the personal GitHub repository, push the initial structure, open a test pull request, and obtain a green CI run without deployment steps or runtime secrets.

**Preflight pass:** every tool exists, every local service starts, the selected AI CLI completes a session and preserves its transcript, required ports are free, and the laptop retains at least 15 GB of free space after images are installed.

## Daily AI session and submission contract

One **primary** AI session per day, from initial framing through review (extra sessions may support but don't replace it).

**Input pack** (before the session):

1. Objective: the observable result required today.
2. Starting state: what exists, what works, and what is missing.
3. Authority: public documentation and local synthetic artifacts the AI may rely on.
4. Scope: files, components, and decisions included today.
5. Constraints: security, architecture, time, data, and tool boundaries.
6. Non-goals: work that must remain outside the session.
7. Evidence required: artifacts, tests, traces, and explanations needed for acceptance.
8. Stop conditions: missing evidence, ambiguous decisions, or unsafe actions that require human judgment.

**JSONL:** export the primary session as unedited JSONL (no rewritten summary). Preserve user/assistant messages, tool calls, tool results, errors, corrections, approvals in order. If native format differs, export it plus a lossless JSONL conversion.

| File | Required content |
|---|---|
| `day-N-session.jsonl` | Complete primary AI session in chronological order |
| `day-N-inputs.md` | The eight input-pack fields supplied to the AI |
| `day-N-artifacts.md` | Artifact names, revisions, evidence links, and test commands |
| `day-N-review.md` | Claims accepted, claims rejected, corrections made, and unresolved gaps |
| `day-N-score.md` | Assessor score with evidence for every awarded point |

Each JSONL record keeps native event type and timestamp where available. A normalized conversion must include `timestamp`, `role`, `type`, `content`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_output`, and `evidence_refs` when those fields apply. Redact credentials and sensitive values, but record that a redaction occurred. Do not remove failed attempts or critical feedback.

### Daily scoring method

The assessor reviews the built artifact and the JSONL together. Each day is worth 10 points:

| Dimension | Points | Award rule |
|---|---|---|
| Planned outcome | 3 | Required artifact works and satisfies the day's stop condition |
| Engineering evidence | 2 | Tests, traces, citations, or negative results directly prove the claims |
| AI session quality | 2 | Prompt inputs are complete, authority is bounded, and corrections show independent judgment |
| Day test | 2 | The named test passes without hidden assistance |
| Teach-back | 1 | Candidate explains the decision, limitation, and next step clearly |

**Daily pass:** 8 of 10 or higher, with the planned outcome, day test, JSONL transcript, and review file all accepted. Missing or edited JSONL makes the day incomplete and produces no score until corrected.

---

# Week one — Product and system foundations

## Day 1: User problem and product outcome

**Learn:** interview structure and jobs to be done; present workflow, pain, constraints, decision makers; value hypothesis, baseline, target, guardrail measure; user journey, acceptance criteria, non-goals, product risk; requested feature vs. underlying problem.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Frame | 30 min | Write the vague request, then list the people affected, current behavior, pain, constraint, and unknowns. Do not propose a feature yet. | One-page discovery canvas |
| 2. Interview | 45 min | Ask a peer to role-play the requester. Use only open questions for the first 15 minutes. Separate observed facts from assumptions afterward. | Interview notes with facts and assumptions marked |
| 3. Measure | 45 min | Define a baseline, target, leading measure, and guardrail. State how each measure would be collected. | Four-measure table |
| 4. Slice | 60 min | Draw the present journey and desired journey. Select the smallest change that produces observable value within the capstone. | Before-and-after journey plus non-goals |
| 5. Review | 30 min | Ask an AI agent to challenge the brief for hidden assumptions. Accept a finding only after you can explain the evidence behind it. | Corrected brief and review log |

**Stop condition:** another person can read the brief and state the user, problem, measurable result, first slice, and explicit non-goals without asking for missing context.

**Build:** a product brief for a synthetic AI engineering operations workspace (user submits a product objective, follows a governed engineering run, reviews evidence, approves consequential steps). The brief must include: users and affected stakeholders; current workflow and pain; business outcome and baseline; target measure and guardrail measure; smallest valuable slice; assumptions, risks, and non-goals; observable acceptance criteria.

**Day 1 test:** You receive a vague request: "Add an AI dashboard." Conduct a 20-minute discovery interview and return a problem statement, outcome, first experiment, and evidence plan. Pass when the solution is smaller and more measurable than the original request.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a product-discovery coach and critical reviewer. My objective is to turn the supplied vague request into a measurable problem statement and smallest valuable experiment. Inputs: interview notes, present workflow, affected users, assumptions, constraints, baseline candidates, and non-goals. Ask one question at a time until the problem, baseline, target, guardrail, and evidence source are explicit. Label every statement as observed fact, stakeholder claim, inference, or assumption. Do not propose a feature until the problem and measure are accepted. End by auditing the final brief against today's stop condition."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blind-brief comprehension | Give the brief to a reviewer who did not attend the interview; record whether they can state user, problem, baseline, target, slice, and non-goals | 6 of 6 stated correctly | 2 |
| Evidence classification | Count material claims and claims correctly labeled as fact, claim, inference, or assumption | 100% classified | 2 |
| Measure quality | Reviewer checks baseline source, target, collection method, and guardrail | 4 of 4 present | 2 |
| Scope reduction | Compare requested scope with first experiment and record excluded work | Smaller executable slice with at least three non-goals | 1 |
| Discovery test | Run the 20-minute exercise and score required outputs | All four outputs accepted | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL completeness and compare accepted AI suggestions with corrections | Complete JSONL plus at least one independently checked suggestion | 2 |

## Day 2: AI engineering and evidence

**Learn:** Claude Code / Codex CLI working patterns; minimal authoritative context; observations vs. inferences vs. assumptions vs. unknowns; repository mapping and source citation; architecture decisions and alternatives; task decomposition, scope, permissions, approvals; independent review of plausible AI mistakes.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Prepare | 30 min | Choose a small public repository with tests and a clear entry point. Record its exact revision and the questions you need answered. | Context manifest |
| 2. Map | 60 min | Ask one AI tool to map entry points, components, calls, data, and tests. Require a file and symbol citation for every claim. | Evidence-linked system map |
| 3. Cross-check | 45 min | Give the same bounded question to a second tool without the first answer. Compare agreement, conflict, and omissions. | Comparison table |
| 4. Adversarial review | 45 min | Insert five false or unsupported claims into a copy of the report. Have the candidate review it without revealing their locations. | Findings with corrected evidence |
| 5. Delegate | 60 min | Write one agent task containing objective, authority, scope, constraints, non-goals, completion proof, and stop conditions. Review the result line by line. | Task contract and acceptance record |

**Stop condition:** every material claim is traceable to primary evidence, every disagreement is settled, and no AI conclusion is accepted because it sounds plausible.

**Build:** two separate Claude Code or Codex CLI sessions on a small open-source app. The first produces a component map, runtime flow, ownership map, test map, and ten evidence-linked claims. The second independently reviews an AI-generated report containing planted errors.

**Day 2 test:** Identify all planted unsupported claims. For each one, show the primary evidence, explain the error, and correct the conclusion. Pass only with zero missed high-impact claims.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as an evidence-bound codebase analyst. Objective: map this public repository at revision [REVISION]. Questions: [QUESTIONS]. Scope: [PATHS]. For every claim, cite the exact file and symbol or command output. Separate observation, inference, assumption, and unknown. Do not fill gaps from convention. Produce component, runtime, ownership, and test maps. End with contradictions, missing evidence, and a confidence table that I can independently verify."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Planted-error recall | Divide planted errors found by total planted errors | 100%, with no missed high-impact claim | 2 |
| Review precision | Divide valid findings by all findings raised | At least 90% | 1 |
| Citation validity | Open every cited file, symbol, or command result and count direct support | 10 of 10 claims directly supported | 2 |
| Map coverage | Check entry point, component, call, data, and test maps | 5 of 5 maps complete | 2 |
| Delegation contract | Check the seven required task fields | 7 of 7 present | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate complete JSONL and identify where the candidate rejected or corrected the AI | Complete JSONL plus at least two justified corrections | 2 |

## Day 3: Product experience and frontend

**Learn:** workflow design before data design; React + TypeScript fundamentals; accessible forms, navigation, focus, labels, keyboard; responsive design and design-system reuse; loading, empty, populated, failure, unavailable, recovery states; fixtures for development, real producer required before release.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Study | 45 min | Complete the React TypeScript guide and review MDN guidance for forms, keyboard interaction, focus, and semantic HTML. | Notes with five rules applied today |
| 2. Model | 45 min | Draw the user journey and enumerate loading, empty, populated, validation, permission, failure, unavailable, and recovery states. | State inventory |
| 3. Prototype | 90 min | Build the workflow with typed synthetic fixtures. Keep state transitions visible and use semantic controls before styling. | Working responsive flow |
| 4. Accessibility pass | 45 min | Complete the flow with keyboard only, inspect focus order and labels, then repeat at a narrow viewport. | Accessibility findings and fixes |
| 5. Review | 30 min | Ask AI for a product and accessibility review. Verify each finding in the browser before changing code. | Settled review log |

Public references: React with TypeScript, MDN accessibility.

**Stop condition:** a new user can complete the flow without explanation in keyboard-only and narrow-screen tests, and every defined state has a visible design.

**Build:** the engineering-operations workflow in React with synthetic fixtures: objective intake, run status, evidence review, policy findings, failed tool state, and approval before a consequential action.

**Day 3 test:** A reviewer must complete the workflow using keyboard only and a narrow viewport. Pass when every action and state is visible, understandable, and recoverable.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a product-design and accessibility coach. Objective: implement the supplied user journey in React and TypeScript. Inputs: journey, state inventory, acceptance criteria, design constraints, and synthetic data shapes. First identify missing states and actions. Then guide implementation in small checkpoints. Require semantic controls, visible focus, labels, keyboard operation, responsive behavior, and recovery paths. Do not accept screenshots as proof of interaction. End with a test script covering every state."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Journey completion | Observe a new reviewer completing the primary task without help | Completed without intervention | 2 |
| State coverage | Divide implemented states by the approved state inventory | 100% | 2 |
| Keyboard coverage | Execute every action without a pointer and record failures | 100% operable | 2 |
| Narrow viewport | Run the journey at 360 CSS pixels and record overflow or hidden actions | Zero blocking defects | 1 |
| Recovery | Trigger each failure state and observe a usable recovery action | All recovery paths work | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and verify the candidate tested AI findings in the browser | Complete JSONL plus evidence for every accepted finding | 2 |

## Day 4: API contract and backend

**Learn:** HTTP, JSON, REST semantics, structured errors; OpenAPI as the browser-to-server contract; generated TypeScript clients; Go service structure, validation, context, errors, tests; authn, authz, pagination, idempotency, compatibility; why a browser never receives a datastore credential or driver.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Contract | 60 min | Convert every UI action and state into an OpenAPI operation, schema, status code, and structured error. Define pagination and idempotency where needed. | Valid OpenAPI document |
| 2. Generate | 30 min | Generate the TypeScript client. Remove handwritten request and response types that duplicate the contract. | Generated client used by the UI |
| 3. Implement | 90 min | Build the Go handlers with validation, server-derived identity, context propagation, typed errors, and no datastore access from the browser. | Running API and handler tests |
| 4. Trace | 30 min | For each UI action, record operation, authorization decision, data effect, response, and displayed state. | Action-to-contract matrix |
| 5. Break deliberately | 30 min | Change one required field or response shape and prove that validation, generation, compilation, or a contract test catches it. | Captured failing and passing result |

Public references: OpenAPI specification, A Tour of Go.

**Stop condition:** the browser uses only the generated client, all actions map to documented operations, and a breaking change fails before deployment.

**Build:** the OpenAPI contract for the Day 3 experience, a stateless Go API, and the frontend client generated from the contract.

**Day 4 test:** Trace each user action to an API operation, authorization decision, data effect, and response. Introduce one breaking contract change and demonstrate that the compatibility or build gate catches it.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as an API-contract coach and Go reviewer. Objective: turn the approved interface into an OpenAPI contract, generated TypeScript client, and stateless Go API. Inputs: action-state matrix, identity rule, data effects, errors, pagination, and idempotency needs. Work contract first. For each operation require validation, authorization, response, error, and test behavior. Flag any handwritten browser type that duplicates the contract. End with one deliberate breaking change and the gate expected to catch it."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Action coverage | Divide UI actions mapped to operations by total UI actions | 100% | 2 |
| Contract validity | Run OpenAPI validation and client generation | Both succeed with zero warnings | 1 |
| Generated-client use | Search browser request paths and duplicated transport types | All API calls use generated client; zero duplicate types | 1 |
| Handler behavior | Run validation, authorization, success, and structured-error tests | All required cases pass | 2 |
| Breaking-change detection | Apply the planned incompatible change and capture the failing gate | Failure occurs before deployment | 2 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and trace AI claims to specification or tests | Complete JSONL with no unsupported accepted claim | 2 |

## Day 5: Data authority, tenancy, and security

**Learn:** PostgreSQL tables, constraints, indexes, transactions, row-level security; server-derived tenant/account scope; Redis as a bounded read model, not hidden authority; cache coverage, freshness, invalidation, partial-result declaration; evidence files, simulated expiring access, retention, deletion, audit; threat modeling, secrets, least privilege, consent, approval boundaries.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Authority map | 45 min | List each data class, authoritative store, writer, readers, retention rule, and recovery source. Mark every trust boundary. | Authority and data-flow diagram |
| 2. Relational model | 75 min | Create tables, constraints, indexes, and transactions. Enable row-level security and design a default-deny policy for synthetic organizations. | Schema and migration |
| 3. Bounded read | 45 min | Add one Redis read model with maximum cardinality, freshness, invalidation, and explicit partial-coverage fields. | Read contract and bound calculation |
| 4. Threat model | 45 min | Identify assets, actors, entry points, threats, controls, and residual risk. Include client-supplied scope, leaked links, stale cache, and prompt injection. | Reviewed threat model |
| 5. Attack | 45 min | Run negative tests for cross-organization reads and writes, scope substitution, expired evidence access, and stale cached data. | Negative-test transcript |

Public references: PostgreSQL row security, OWASP threat modeling.

**Stop condition:** every data class has one authority and every attempted boundary violation fails predictably without leaking sensitive information.

**Build:** PostgreSQL account isolation, one Redis-backed bounded read, a local-directory adapter for synthetic evidence, a threat model, and an authority map.

**Day 5 test:** Attempt cross-account reads and writes, client-supplied account substitution, stale-cache reads, and unauthorized evidence access. Pass when every attempt fails predictably and leaves useful, non-sensitive evidence.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a data-authority and security reviewer. Objective: design and test organization isolation, one bounded Redis read, and protected evidence storage. Inputs: data classes, actors, trust boundaries, schema, read requirements, retention, and threat assumptions. Require one authority and writer per data class, server-derived scope, default-deny row security, declared cache bounds, and expiring evidence access. Challenge the design with cross-scope, stale-data, leaked-link, and prompt-injection cases. End with executable negative tests."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Authority coverage | Count data classes with authority, writer, readers, retention, and recovery source | 100% complete | 1 |
| Isolation negatives | Run cross-scope read, write, and scope-substitution tests | 3 of 3 denied | 2 |
| Evidence access | Test unauthorized, expired, and valid access | Unauthorized and expired denied; valid allowed | 1 |
| Cache contract | Verify maximum rows, freshness, invalidation, and partial-coverage fields | 4 of 4 explicit and tested | 2 |
| Threat treatment | Count high threats with preventive or detective control and verification | 100% of high threats covered | 2 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and inspect handling of sensitive inputs and rejected recommendations | Complete JSONL, zero sensitive values, justified review | 2 |

## End of week one checkpoint

| Evidence | Required state |
|---|---|
| Product brief | Reviewed and measurable |
| AI analysis | Every claim linked to primary evidence |
| Frontend workflow | Complete across all states |
| OpenAPI and Go API | Generated client connected |
| Data and threat model | Tenant isolation proven negatively |

Checkpoint result: Continue / Remediate before week two
Blocking gaps: __________

---

# Week two — Delivery and operational ownership

## Day 6: Durable work and provider integrations

**Learn:** verified webhook ingress; workers, leases, heartbeats, health, backpressure; idempotency, deduplication, transactional outbox and inbox; timeouts, rate limits, circuit breakers, bounded retries; process death, duplicate delivery, partial effects, recovery; provider adapters vs. duplicated product implementations.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Define events | 45 min | Specify webhook authenticity, event identity, accepted response, durable receipt, and the user-visible outcome. | Event contract and sequence diagram |
| 2. Make effects safe | 60 min | Add inbox deduplication, an outbox, idempotency keys, lease ownership, heartbeat, and terminal outcome recording. | Durable state model |
| 3. Implement | 75 min | Build the signed ingress, worker, and provider adapter against a controllable stub. Expose worker and queue health. | Running end-to-end path |
| 4. Inject failures | 60 min | Exercise duplicate delivery, rate limit, timeout, process death, and external success followed by local failure. | Failure matrix with observed results |
| 5. Prove recovery | 30 min | Restart the worker and reconcile durable state. Confirm that work completes once and external effects do not repeat. | Recovery trace |

**Stop condition:** every injected failure reaches a deterministic state, recovery needs no manual data repair, and no consequential effect occurs twice.

**Build:** a signed webhook and background job that calls a provider stub, records a durable outcome, and updates the user-visible state.

**Day 6 test:** Inject duplicate webhook delivery, provider timeout, rate limiting, worker death, and a completed external effect followed by local failure. Pass when recovery is deterministic and no external effect occurs twice.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a distributed-workflow designer and failure-test reviewer. Objective: implement signed webhook ingress and durable background work against a controllable provider stub. Inputs: event contract, state model, external effects, retry policy, rate limits, and user-visible outcomes. Require deduplication, idempotency, outbox or inbox behavior, leases, heartbeats, terminal states, and recovery. For every design choice, identify the failure it prevents. End with executable fault-injection steps and expected durable state."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signature and receipt | Send valid, invalid, and replayed webhook inputs | Valid accepted; invalid denied; replay deduplicated | 1 |
| Failure matrix | Run duplicate, timeout, rate limit, worker death, and partial-effect cases | 5 of 5 reach expected state | 3 |
| External-effect count | Record provider-stub calls by idempotency key | Exactly one consequential effect per key | 2 |
| Recovery | Restart after each interrupted state and compare final state with expected state | 100% deterministic recovery | 2 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and verify every accepted retry or recovery claim with a fault test | Complete JSONL and direct evidence | 2 |

## Day 7: AI product behavior

**Learn:** model selection and model-independent workflow design; prompt and tool contracts; structured outputs and validation; retrieval boundaries and provenance; evaluation datasets and expected outcomes; hallucination, latency, spend, safety controls; human approval for consequential actions.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Define the contract | 45 min | Specify permitted inputs, structured output schema, tools, denied actions, budget, latency target, and approval boundary. | AI behavior contract |
| 2. Build evaluations | 60 min | Create at least 20 cases spanning normal, ambiguous, unsupported, hostile, and tool-failure inputs. State the expected decision for each. | Versioned evaluation set |
| 3. Implement | 75 min | Connect the model through structured output validation and least-privilege tools. Reject invalid output rather than parsing guesses. | Working bounded workflow |
| 4. Attack | 45 min | Test direct and indirect prompt injection, unauthorized tool requests, fabricated evidence, budget exhaustion, and unsafe action proposals. | Adversarial test results |
| 5. Measure | 30 min | Record task success, unsafe-action rate, structured-output failures, latency, and cost. Review failures before changing prompts or models. | Evaluation report |

Public references: OWASP prompt-injection prevention, OWASP AI threat modeling.

**Stop condition:** all safety-critical cases pass, invalid output is rejected, tool authority is enforced outside the model, and every consequential action requires approval.

**Build:** one AI workflow that analyzes an engineering objective and proposes a bounded implementation step, with structured output, tool authorization, evaluation cases, cost budget, latency budget, and approval before action.

**Day 7 test:** Classify injected failures as model, data, prompt, tool, policy, workflow, or infrastructure failures. Select the correct correction for each. Pass when no failure is hidden with a blind retry.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as an AI-product evaluation coach and adversarial reviewer. Objective: implement a bounded model workflow for [TASK]. Inputs: allowed data, structured-output schema, tools, denied actions, approval rule, evaluation cases, latency limit, and cost limit. Keep tool authorization outside the model. Classify failures as model, data, prompt, tool, policy, workflow, or infrastructure. Do not prescribe a retry until the failure class proves it is safe. End with evaluation results and the correction selected for every failure."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation completion | Run all 20 or more versioned cases and store actual versus expected result | 100% executed | 1 |
| Safety-critical success | Count passed authorization, injection, and consequential-action cases | 100% pass | 2 |
| Task success | Divide accepted normal outcomes by normal evaluation cases | At least 90% | 1 |
| Structured output | Count schema-valid outputs and confirm invalid output is rejected | All accepted output valid; invalid rejected | 1 |
| Failure classification | Independently review injected failure labels and corrections | All classes and corrections accepted | 1 |
| Budgets and approval | Record p95 latency, cost, and action attempts with and without approval | Within limits; denied first and allowed second | 2 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and record prompt, model, tool, policy, and evaluation revisions | Complete reproducible package | 2 |

## Day 8: Containers and local deployment

**Learn:** container images and immutable artifact identity; local service composition, health checks, configuration, secrets; process identity, least privilege, ports, volumes, private networks; Docker Compose configuration and dependency ordering; restart behavior, local persistence, artifact verification; reported health vs. correct behavior.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Package | 60 min | Build immutable images, run them as a non-root user, and separate configuration from secrets. Record source revision and image digest. | Image manifest and local run proof |
| 2. Compose | 45 min | Define local services, private networks, loopback ports, volumes, health checks, configuration, and secret references in Docker Compose. | Reviewed Compose configuration |
| 3. Apply locally | 45 min | Build and start the stack with Docker Compose. Observe startup order, health, logs, and served behavior. | Local startup transcript |
| 4. Restart | 30 min | Stop and restart selected services. Verify persistent state, dependency recovery, and clear failure behavior. | Restart and recovery results |
| 5. Verify identity | 30 min | Trace approved source to local image digest, Compose configuration, running container, and response. | Artifact-identity chain |

Public reference: Docker Compose.

**Stop condition:** the exact approved local image and configuration are running, restart behavior is proven, and served behavior is independently verified.

**Build:** containerize the capstone and run the complete stack on the laptop with Docker Compose.

**Day 8 test:** Trace approved source to image, Compose configuration, running container, and served behavior. Detect one container that reports healthy but runs the wrong artifact or configuration.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a local-deployment coach and verifier. Objective: package the capstone and run it on this laptop with Docker Compose. Inputs: source revision, image requirements, local configuration, secret references, ports, volumes, health checks, and acceptance path. Guide me from source to local image to Compose configuration to running container. Treat reported health as one signal only. Reject any hosted service or remote runtime. End with an artifact-identity procedure and a wrong-artifact experiment."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Image identity | Record source revision, image digest, and runtime digest | Exact match across all three | 2 |
| Compose review | Check identity, health, ports, volumes, least privilege, and secret references | 6 of 6 accepted | 2 |
| Local startup | Record image, configuration, service health, logs, and served response | All five accepted | 1 |
| GitHub CI | Push the reviewed commit and inspect required checks | All required checks pass; no deployment job exists | 1 |
| Restart recovery | Restart the API and one stateful dependency | Behavior and data recover as designed | 1 |
| Wrong-artifact detection | Deploy healthy wrong identity or configuration and run verification | Mismatch detected before acceptance | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and link every deployment claim to command or runtime evidence | Complete JSONL and evidence chain | 2 |

## Day 9: Observability and incident response

**Learn:** structured logs, simple counters, request IDs, context propagation; service-level concepts, useful symptoms, meaningful thresholds; first-divergence diagnosis; incident impact, containment, root cause, correction, verification; recovery objectives, simple cost estimates, runbooks.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Add signals | 60 min | Propagate one request ID across browser, API, database call, worker, local provider stub, and returned result. Write structured logs to a local file. | Correlated log sequence |
| 2. Define health | 30 min | Choose one user-centered success ratio and one response-time threshold. Calculate both from a small local test run. | Hand-checked metrics summary |
| 3. Prepare response | 30 min | Write a one-page runbook containing symptom, relevant logs, first checks, containment, and verification. | Local runbook |
| 4. Diagnose | 60 min | Ask another person to enable one provided failure switch without naming it. Follow the request ID and logs to the first divergence. | Incident timeline and causal chain |
| 5. Correct and verify | 30 min | Fix the cause, rerun the same curl or browser steps, and compare the before-and-after logs. | Before-and-after evidence |

**Stop condition:** the candidate can identify impact, first divergence, causal mechanism, correction, and repeat-test proof using only local logs and simple measurements.

**Build:** request IDs and structured logs across the local flow, one metrics summary, and one short incident runbook.

**Day 9 test:** Diagnose an injected failure without being told where it is. Pass when you find the first divergent signal, explain the causal mechanism, correct the root cause, and verify the correction at the same observation points.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a local incident-diagnosis coach. Objective: use request IDs, structured local logs, and simple counters to diagnose an unknown injected failure. Inputs: expected request path, log fields, service boundaries, success ratio, response-time threshold, and runbook. Ask me for observed signals before suggesting causes. Maintain a hypothesis table with confirming and falsifying evidence. Identify the first divergence, causal mechanism, correction, and repeat-test verification. Do not require an observability platform or infer success from code alone."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Log continuity | Count expected boundaries carrying the same request ID | 100% of browser-to-result boundaries | 2 |
| Metric calculation | Recompute success ratio and response-time result from raw local observations | Values agree with the summary | 1 |
| Runbook usefulness | Follow the runbook from the visible symptom without hidden knowledge | Reaches useful first checks | 1 |
| First-divergence accuracy | Compare diagnosis with injected fault location and causal chain | First divergence and mechanism correct | 2 |
| Same-signal verification | Repeat the original observation after correction | Symptom and divergence both absent | 2 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and inspect hypothesis changes against evidence | Complete JSONL with no unsupported leap | 2 |

## Day 10: Capstone, review, and readiness board

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Freeze | 30 min | Stop feature work. Record the exact source revision, image digest, configuration revision, open findings, and known limitations. | Release candidate record |
| 2. Review | 90 min | Run product, frontend, backend, architecture, security, test, and simplicity reviews. Classify every finding and close all high-severity items. | Settled review ledger |
| 3. Rehearse | 60 min | Run the complete user path, one denied action, one provider failure, and one recovery. Capture traces and visible results. | Demonstration evidence pack |
| 4. Present | 45 min | Explain the problem, outcome, workflow, architecture, AI controls, live proof, limitations, cost, and next decision in that order. | Fifteen-minute demonstration |
| 5. Assess | 45 min | Complete the readiness board from observable evidence. Record gaps as specific preparation work rather than awarding partial credit without proof. | Signed scorecard and preparation plan |

**Stop condition:** the reviewed artifact is the deployed artifact, the complete path and recovery are demonstrated live, and every readiness score links to evidence.

**Morning:**
1. Run architecture, security, frontend, backend, test, and simplicity reviews.
2. Close all high-severity findings.
3. Re-run the required tests.
4. Deploy the exact reviewed artifact.
5. Capture one complete local request-ID and log sequence.

**Afternoon:**
1. Present the user problem and measured outcome.
2. Demonstrate the product and failure recovery.
3. Explain the architecture and authority boundaries.
4. Show how AI agents were directed and checked.
5. Complete the scored readiness interview.

**Day 10 decision** — the result is one of:
- **Qualified:** has demonstrated the required pre-join foundation.
- **Qualified with targeted preparation:** has named gaps that must be closed before formal onboarding.
- **Not yet qualified:** must close critical gaps before taking the role.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a release-readiness coordinator and skeptical review chair. Objective: determine whether the exact capstone artifact is ready for demonstration and qualification review. Inputs: accepted scope, source revision, image digest, Compose revision, CI results, local test results, review findings, correlated logs, incident evidence, costs, limitations, and readiness criteria. Build an evidence ledger. Do not award credit for claims without an artifact or observed result. Identify contradictions and open high-severity findings. End with a demonstration order and a proposed score that the human assessor must independently approve."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Review closure | Count open high-severity findings across required reviews | Zero open | 2 |
| Artifact match | Compare reviewed source, built digest, configured revision, and running digest | Exact match | 1 |
| Live path and recovery | Run the primary journey, one denied action, and one provider failure with recovery | All three behave as designed | 2 |
| Evidence coverage | Divide readiness claims with direct evidence by total readiness claims | 100% | 1 |
| Demonstration | Score problem, outcome, workflow, architecture, controls, proof, limitation, and next decision | 8 of 8 within 15 minutes | 1 |
| Scoring integrity | Independently recompute daily and final scores from evidence | No unsupported awarded point | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL and compare the proposed score with the human-approved score | Complete JSONL with differences explained | 2 |

---

# Capstone — AI engineering operations workspace

One synthetic product proves the complete learning path without internal source code, production information, or private architecture.

## Required capstone system

| Surface | Minimum capability |
|---|---|
| User application | React and TypeScript, responsive, accessible, all data states |
| API | Stateless Go service with published OpenAPI and generated client |
| Identity | Locally signed synthetic tokens and server-derived account context |
| Operational data | PostgreSQL with database-enforced account isolation |
| Read path | Redis-backed bounded list with declared coverage and freshness |
| Evidence | Local-directory adapter with simulated retention and expiring access |
| Ingress | Signature-verified webhook from a laptop-hosted provider stub |
| Background work | Durable worker with local provider-stub adapters and health |
| Correctness | Idempotency, outbox, deduplication, explicit failure states |
| AI workflow | Claude Code or Codex CLI engineering session, local deterministic runtime stub, evaluation corpus, budget, and approval |
| Orchestration | Objective, decision, plan, execution, review, and verification states |
| Governance | Synthetic policy finding that blocks an unsafe proposed change |
| Delivery | Personal GitHub repository, green CI, local images, and Docker Compose on the laptop |
| Operations | Request IDs, structured logs, simple metrics summary, runbook, cost estimate |

## Required proof

- User problem and measurable outcome
- User journey, approved interface, and every state
- Architecture decision with viable alternatives
- Threat model and authority map
- Decision-frozen implementation plan
- AI task contracts and returned evidence
- Reviewed code with no open high-severity findings
- Contract, isolation, failure, and recovery tests
- Local Compose deployment and exact artifact identity
- Personal GitHub repository with reviewed daily pull requests and green CI
- Correlated local evidence from user action through background result to the UI
- Injected incident and same-signal verification
- User-oriented demonstration

**Code completion is not product completion:** the capstone is complete only after local deployment, an end-to-end behavior check, a simulated failure, verified recovery, and a user-oriented demonstration.

## How to direct AI work

Every task sent to an AI agent must state:

| Field | Required content |
|---|---|
| Objective | One observable outcome |
| Authority | Current sources and facts that govern the work |
| Scope | Exact component, files, or decision surface |
| Constraints | Product, security, architecture, and compatibility invariants |
| Non-goals | Work the agent must not absorb |
| Completion | Tests, review state, live proof, and artifact required |
| Escalation | Ambiguity or reality divergence that stops execution |

Workflow phases: **Research** (collect current evidence, expose unknowns) → **Decide** (compare alternatives, record the architecture) → **Plan** (freeze scope, dependencies, tests, deletion gates, proof) → **Implement** (execute bounded work without inventing design) → **Review** (challenge correctness, security, architecture, tests, product quality, simplicity) → **Verify** (deploy and prove behavior through the real observation chain).

---

# Qualification — Readiness tests

A 100-point board based on observable work. Every critical test (marked `*`) must pass independently.

## Scoring rules

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| No evidence | 0 points |
| Guided | Completes only with step-by-step help, half points at most |
| Independent | Completes and explains without intervention, full points |
| Teaching | Handles variants and coaches another engineer, distinction noted |

- **Qualified:** 80 or more points, every critical test passed, capstone accepted, no automatic failure.
- **Qualified with targeted preparation:** 70 to 79 points, all critical tests passed, written preparation plan in place.
- **Not yet qualified:** below 70, any critical test failed, capstone rejected, or automatic failure present.

### A. Product ownership, 15 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Discover the real problem | Interview, workflow, users, constraints, assumptions | 3 |
| P2 | Define measurable value | Baseline, target, leading and guardrail measures | 3 |
| P3* | Freeze acceptance | Testable behavior including failure and recovery | 3 |
| P4 | Choose the smallest valuable slice | Scope and explicit non-goals | 3 |
| P5 | Demonstrate and learn | Outcome demo, feedback, next decision | 3 |

Score: ____ / 15

### B. AI engineering, 20 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI1 | Build a minimal context pack | Sources, freshness, conflicts, unknowns | 4 |
| AI2* | Verify AI claims | Planted errors found and corrected from primary evidence | 4 |
| AI3 | Compare designs | Viable alternatives, tradeoffs, evidence, decision | 4 |
| AI4* | Delegate bounded work | Objective, scope, constraints, proof, escalation | 4 |
| AI5 | Run the complete workflow | Separate research, decision, plan, execution, review, verification | 4 |

Score: ____ / 20

### C. Architecture and implementation, 20 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Map the complete system | Components, writers, readers, contracts, flow | 4 |
| A2* | Protect tenant authority | Server-derived scope and negative isolation tests | 4 |
| A3 | Assign data authority | One authority per class, bounded reads, recovery effects | 4 |
| A4* | Design failure behavior | Duplicate, timeout, death, partial effect, stale state | 4 |
| A5* | Review AI-produced code | Substantive correctness, security, concurrency, simplicity findings | 4 |

Score: ____ / 20

### D. Delivery and operations, 20 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| O1 | Package reproducibly | Immutable, configured, secret-free artifact | 4 |
| O2 | Deploy locally | Reviewed Compose configuration and observed startup | 4 |
| O3 | Verify artifact identity | Running source and configuration match approval | 4 |
| O4* | Prove local behavior | Correlated local evidence to user-visible result | 4 |
| O5* | Diagnose an incident | First divergence, cause, correction, same-signal proof | 4 |

Score: ____ / 20

### E. Security and governance, 15 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1* | Protect secrets and production data | No sensitive value in prompts, code, logs, or artifacts | 3 |
| S2* | Enforce identity and authorization | Principal, tenant, target, action, elevation | 3 |
| S3 | Threat-model the product | Assets, actors, boundaries, abuse, controls, risk | 3 |
| S4 | Govern evidence and deletion | Consent, retention, access, audit, deletion | 3 |
| S5 | Bound AI authority | Permissions, approvals, budgets, policy, lineage | 3 |

Score: ____ / 15

### F. Communication and ownership, 10 points

| ID | Test | Evidence | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | Explain at user altitude | Outcome, behavior, limitation, next decision | 2 |
| L2 | Explain at engineering altitude | Contract, authority, failure, proof | 2 |
| L3 | Make ownership visible | Decision owner, worker, reviewer, operator | 2 |
| L4 | Manage tradeoffs | Value, speed, reliability, security, cost | 2 |
| L5 | Improve the system | Learning or runbook updated from evidence | 2 |

Score: ____ / 10

## Critical checklist

- [ ] P3: acceptance is observable and covers failure states
- [ ] AI2: AI claims are verified against primary evidence
- [ ] AI4: agent work has exact authority and mutation boundaries
- [ ] A2: tenant authority is server-derived and tested negatively
- [ ] A4: common failures have deterministic behavior
- [ ] A5: AI-generated code receives substantive human review
- [ ] O4: behavior is proven through a local end-to-end check
- [ ] O5: incident diagnosis finds and verifies the root cause
- [ ] S1: secrets and production data stay inside approved boundaries
- [ ] S2: identity and authorization protect every consequential action

## Automatic failures

- trusting an AI conclusion without checking its source;
- exposing a datastore driver or credential to the browser;
- accepting tenant authority from an untrusted client field;
- placing secrets or real production data into unapproved model context;
- bypassing a failed security, CI, deployment, or review control;
- changing architecture silently during implementation;
- using retries or longer timeouts to hide an ambiguous machine contract;
- declaring completion from tests while the live path remains unobserved;
- shipping known broken behavior, orphan code, or unexplained data loss;
- optimizing agent activity while ignoring product outcome, reliability, or cost.

## Day 10 readiness decision

| Area | Available | Score |
|---|---|---|
| Product ownership | 15 | ____ |
| AI engineering | 20 | ____ |
| Architecture and implementation | 20 | ____ |
| Delivery and operations | 20 | ____ |
| Security and governance | 15 | ____ |
| Communication and ownership | 10 | ____ |
| **Total** | **100** | ____ |

Critical tests passed: ____ / 10
Capstone accepted: Yes / No
Automatic failure present: Yes / No
Decision: Qualified / Qualified with targeted preparation / Not yet qualified
Assessor: ______
Date: __________
Targeted coaching plan:
1.
2.
3.

---

# After qualification

Qualification establishes readiness for formal onboarding and supervised product work. Formal onboarding sequence:

1. **NebCore foundation** — platform contracts, access model, delivery path, data boundaries, operating standards.
2. **NebPilot workflow** — governed path from objective through decision, plan, execution, review, verification.
3. **NebGuard governance** — how policy, evidence, and review controls protect engineering changes.
4. **Project onboarding** — source, architecture, security boundaries, operating procedures for assigned work.
5. **Supervised ownership** — bounded product work with review before independent ownership is granted.

Passing does not grant access to source code, systems, credentials, or private design material.

**Final commitment:** owning product outcomes, not tickets · using AI as a bounded engineering system, not an authority · making architecture and product decisions explicit · protecting identity, tenant data, credentials, consent, and evidence · reviewing generated work with independent judgment · proving live behavior before declaring completion · learning from incidents and improving the system · building reusable foundations only when evidence supports them.

> The goal is not to produce more software. The goal is to own better product outcomes through a trustworthy AI engineering system.

# AI Product Engineering Owner — 10-day learning path (summary)

> Source: `ai-product-engineering-owner-10-day-learning-path.pdf` (Nebinfra Technologies, APSO-10D-2026-001, 2026-09-20, private and confidential).
> Prose is condensed; tables, day tests, AI prompts, and scoring rules are reproduced verbatim.

## Mission

In ten business days, build the evidence needed to qualify for an AI-native product engineering role (the next generation of the AI Forward Engineer) and prepare for formal onboarding. AI agents do a growing share of research, coding, testing, and analysis; you remain accountable for every decision and result.

- **10** business days · **1** synthetic capstone · **100** readiness points · **80** minimum passing score
- Operating principle: *AI can multiply execution. It does not transfer accountability.*
- A Day 10 pass qualifies you for the role; it does not certify independent product ownership. Detailed NebCore training belongs to formal onboarding.

## The role you are preparing for

| Responsibility | The question you must answer |
|---|---|
| Product outcome | What problem are we solving, for whom, and how will success be measured? |
| Product contract | What must the user experience, including loading, empty, failure, and recovery states? |
| Architecture | Where does authority live, how does data move, and how does the system fail? |
| AI engineering | What may agents do, what evidence must they return, and where must a human decide? |
| Delivery | How does an accepted decision become a reviewed, deployed, verified change? |
| Operations | Is the product healthy, secure, affordable, supportable, and improving? |

**Ownership loop:** 01 Discover (user, work, constraint, business result) → 02 Decide (freeze experience, contract, architecture, risks) → 03 Direct (AI agents get bounded objectives and evidence requirements) → 04 Prove (review, test, deploy, trace real behavior) → 05 Improve (measure outcomes, reliability, cost, learning).

## Daily operating rhythm

Full-time intensive, eight focused hours per day.

| Time | Activity | Daily evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 90 minutes | Learn the day's concepts from primary sources | Notes and concept check |
| 3 hours | Build the required capstone slice | Working implementation |
| 90 minutes | Direct an AI agent on bounded work | Task contract and transcript summary |
| 60 minutes | Review AI output adversarially | Findings and corrections |
| 60 minutes | Test and trace the real path | Test result and runtime evidence |
| 30 minutes | Explain the learning back | Short written or recorded teach-back |

Every day ends with a usable artifact. Reading without building does not count as completion.

## Local workstation requirement

All hosting, test traffic, storage, identity simulation, deployment, and operational evidence run on the laptop. No public cloud, hosted DB/object store/identity, remote runtime, public webhook relay, or deployment platform. Internet only for docs, package downloads, the personal GitHub repo + GitHub Actions CI, and an authorized Claude Code or Codex CLI subscription. GitHub stores source, docs, reviews, CI — never the app, its data, model, or runtime dependencies. macOS and Linux only (no Windows, no WSL).

### Laptop capacity

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | 8 logical cores | 12 or more logical cores |
| Memory | 16 GB | 32 GB or more |
| Free SSD space | 60 GB | 100 GB or more |
| Architecture | Apple silicon, x86_64, or Linux arm64 | Apple silicon or Linux x86_64 with supported GPU |
| Network | Internet during setup | Internet during setup; offline-capable during daily tests |

At 16 GB run only the day's services; at 32 GB+ the full stack. Record actual peak memory, disk use, and service startup time during preflight.

### Required local tools

| Area | Required tools | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Shell and source | Bash or Zsh, Git, GitHub CLI, Make, curl, jq, OpenSSL | Automation, version control, pull requests, API probes, JSON processing, signatures |
| Frontend | Current Node.js LTS, Corepack, pnpm, browser developer tools | React build and simple browser checks |
| Backend | Current stable Go toolchain | API, worker, tests, profiling |
| Utility scripting | Python 3.12 or newer and uv | Local scripts, fixtures, JSONL validation |
| Containers | Docker Engine with Compose v2 | All stateful and supporting services |
| AI engineering CLI | Claude Code or Codex CLI with an active authorized subscription | Daily AI engineering sessions and native transcript capture |
| Local checks | Browser, curl, jq, shell scripts, standard project test commands | Simple repeatable behavior and failure checks |

Pin versions (project files or version manager); record every installed version in `workstation-versions.txt`. No unpinned `latest` container tags in submitted work.

### Required personal GitHub repository

Create before Day 1 (private preferred); grant the assessor read access before first submission.

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | Local setup, start, stop, test, reset, and assessment instructions |
| `apps/` | Frontend and Go API source |
| `services/` | Worker and local provider stub |
| `deploy/compose.yaml` | Complete laptop-hosted runtime |
| `docs/day-01/` through `docs/day-10/` | Daily inputs, JSONL, artifacts, review, score, and teach-back |

CI must run formatting or lint checks, frontend tests, Go tests, OpenAPI validation, a production build, and JSONL submission validation. CI must not deploy anything, call a hosted model, or require production credentials; use fixtures and deterministic local substitutes.

Daily work: branch `day-N-topic`, one PR into the default branch. The PR links the five daily submission files, reports the measured score, and includes the CI run. Merge only after required checks pass and the daily review is complete.

### Required laptop-hosted services

| Service | Local implementation | Default binding |
|---|---|---|
| Application UI | React development server or local container | 127.0.0.1:3000 |
| Go API | Local process or container | 127.0.0.1:8080 |
| PostgreSQL | Container with host-local volume | 127.0.0.1:5432 |
| Redis | Container with host-local volume | 127.0.0.1:6379 |
| Evidence files | Project-local directory with generated expiring-link simulation | Local filesystem only |
| Identity simulation | Locally signed synthetic tokens issued by a test helper | No separate identity server |
| Capstone AI adapter | Local deterministic stub or recorded fixture | Application tests without a hosted runtime dependency |
| Provider simulation | Candidate-built signed webhook and failure stub | 127.0.0.1:8090 |
| Operational signals | Structured application logs and a local metrics summary file | Local files and terminal output |

Bind ports to `127.0.0.1`, not `0.0.0.0`. Synthetic credentials stored outside source control. Test data and evidence in a deletable project-local directory.

### Local preflight gate

Before Day 1, submit `workstation-preflight.md` with the command and captured result for each check:

1. Confirm the operating system is macOS or Linux and record CPU architecture.
2. Record CPU count, total memory, and free disk space.
3. Record versions of Git, GitHub CLI, Node.js, pnpm, Go, Python, uv, Docker, Compose, the selected AI CLI, curl, and jq.
4. Start a container and prove it is reachable only through loopback.
5. Authenticate Claude Code or Codex CLI with the candidate's subscription, complete one test session, and locate its native transcript or JSONL export.
6. Build the application images locally and start them with Docker Compose without pulling application images from a remote registry.
7. Start PostgreSQL and Redis; verify health and local persistence. Create the evidence directory and a synthetic signed-token fixture.
8. Prove that all application endpoints resolve to loopback or the private Compose network and that no runtime configuration names an external service.
9. Create the personal GitHub repository, push the initial structure, open a test pull request, and obtain a green CI run without deployment steps or runtime secrets.

**Preflight pass:** every tool exists, every local service starts, the selected AI CLI completes a session and preserves its transcript, required ports are free, and the laptop retains at least 15 GB of free space after images are installed.

## Daily AI session and submission contract

One **primary** AI session per day, from initial framing through review (extra sessions may support but don't replace it).

**Input pack** (before the session):

1. Objective: the observable result required today.
2. Starting state: what exists, what works, and what is missing.
3. Authority: public documentation and local synthetic artifacts the AI may rely on.
4. Scope: files, components, and decisions included today.
5. Constraints: security, architecture, time, data, and tool boundaries.
6. Non-goals: work that must remain outside the session.
7. Evidence required: artifacts, tests, traces, and explanations needed for acceptance.
8. Stop conditions: missing evidence, ambiguous decisions, or unsafe actions that require human judgment.

**JSONL:** export the primary session as unedited JSONL (no rewritten summary). Preserve user/assistant messages, tool calls, tool results, errors, corrections, approvals in order. If native format differs, export it plus a lossless JSONL conversion.

| File | Required content |
|---|---|
| `day-N-session.jsonl` | Complete primary AI session in chronological order |
| `day-N-inputs.md` | The eight input-pack fields supplied to the AI |
| `day-N-artifacts.md` | Artifact names, revisions, evidence links, and test commands |
| `day-N-review.md` | Claims accepted, claims rejected, corrections made, and unresolved gaps |
| `day-N-score.md` | Assessor score with evidence for every awarded point |

Each JSONL record keeps native event type and timestamp where available. A normalized conversion must include `timestamp`, `role`, `type`, `content`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_output`, and `evidence_refs` when those fields apply. Redact credentials and sensitive values, but record that a redaction occurred. Do not remove failed attempts or critical feedback.

### Daily scoring method

The assessor reviews the built artifact and the JSONL together. Each day is worth 10 points:

| Dimension | Points | Award rule |
|---|---|---|
| Planned outcome | 3 | Required artifact works and satisfies the day's stop condition |
| Engineering evidence | 2 | Tests, traces, citations, or negative results directly prove the claims |
| AI session quality | 2 | Prompt inputs are complete, authority is bounded, and corrections show independent judgment |
| Day test | 2 | The named test passes without hidden assistance |
| Teach-back | 1 | Candidate explains the decision, limitation, and next step clearly |

**Daily pass:** 8 of 10 or higher, with the planned outcome, day test, JSONL transcript, and review file all accepted. Missing or edited JSONL makes the day incomplete and produces no score until corrected.

# Week one — Product and system foundations

## Day 1: User problem and product outcome

**Learn:** interview structure and jobs to be done; present workflow, pain, constraints, decision makers; value hypothesis, baseline, target, guardrail measure; user journey, acceptance criteria, non-goals, product risk; requested feature vs. underlying problem.

| Step | Time | Instruction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Frame | 30 min | Write the vague request, then list the people affected, current behavior, pain, constraint, and unknowns. Do not propose a feature yet. | One-page discovery canvas |
| 2. Interview | 45 min | Ask a peer to role-play the requester. Use only open questions for the first 15 minutes. Separate observed facts from assumptions afterward. | Interview notes with facts and assumptions marked |
| 3. Measure | 45 min | Define a baseline, target, leading measure, and guardrail. State how each measure would be collected. | Four-measure table |
| 4. Slice | 60 min | Draw the present journey and desired journey. Select the smallest change that produces observable value within the capstone. | Before-and-after journey plus non-goals |
| 5. Review | 30 min | Ask an AI agent to challenge the brief for hidden assumptions. Accept a finding only after you can explain the evidence behind it. | Corrected brief and review log |

**Stop condition:** another person can read the brief and state the user, problem, measurable result, first slice, and explicit non-goals without asking for missing context.

**Build:** a product brief for a synthetic AI engineering operations workspace (user submits a product objective, follows a governed engineering run, reviews evidence, approves consequential steps). The brief must include: users and affected stakeholders; current workflow and pain; business outcome and baseline; target measure and guardrail measure; smallest valuable slice; assumptions, risks, and non-goals; observable acceptance criteria.

**Day 1 test:** You receive a vague request: "Add an AI dashboard." Conduct a 20-minute discovery interview and return a problem statement, outcome, first experiment, and evidence plan. Pass when the solution is smaller and more measurable than the original request.

**Primary-session prompt:** "Act as a product-discovery coach and critical reviewer. My objective is to turn the supplied vague request into a measurable problem statement and smallest valuable experiment. Inputs: interview notes, present workflow, affected users, assumptions, constraints, baseline candidates, and non-goals. Ask one question at a time until the problem, baseline, target, guardrail, and evidence source are explicit. Label every statement as observed fact, stakeholder claim, inference, or assumption. Do not propose a feature until the problem and measure are accepted. End by auditing the final brief against today's stop condition."

| Measurement | How to collect it | Pass threshold | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blind-brief comprehension | Give the brief to a reviewer who did not attend the interview; record whether they can state user, problem, baseline, target, slice, and non-goals | 6 of 6 stated correctly | 2 |
| Evidence classification | Count material claims and claims correctly labeled as fact, claim, inference, or assumption | 100% classified | 2 |
| Measure quality | Reviewer checks baseline source, target, collection method, and guardrail | 4 of 4 present | 2 |
| Scope reduction | Compare requested scope with first experiment and record excluded work | Smaller executable slice with at least three non-goals | 1 |
| Discovery test | Run the 20-minute exercise and score required outputs | All four outputs accepted | 1 |
| AI submission | Validate JSONL completeness and compare accepted AI suggestions with corrections | Complete JSONL plus at least one independently checked suggestion | 2 |
